About midnight a longboat landed five at the creek mouth: Sparrow (brown coat), four hands with pikes and hand crossbows. At dawn a tall hooded man in a grey cloak came ashore from a second boat and stood two hours on the shed roof watching the road, then went inside. They have hauled a coil of heavy chain and two rowboat anchors from the shed to the far end of the causeway, hidden in the grass: likely a drag-barrier for the culvert. Wren's tell reeds on the stake path were scattered: someone used the stake. Marl lay unseen. The Heron's Tithe herself is not in sight; she may be in the creek behind the shed. Landward reeds are clear; Pell's six guards are moved up quietly. The causeway opens about 2 PM; the wagon is due to start at about 2:30 so it reaches the culvert as the water drops.

You ride up beside the wagon and murmur your warning. Corvin looks at you with real amusement. "A single word, and Pell gags me. I've been threatened by better, and by worse. I'll behave." Pell, riding on his other side, says to the sky that he would enjoy that very much. You give the order to move out, with Kit at your elbow and the six guards falling in behind. You hum the road song quietly, and by the second mile two of the guards are humming it back.

It is half a day to the flats. The country empties out into sea-lavender and gulls, and a little before one in the afternoon you reach the landward end of the Gannet Causeway. The water is dropping, and the causeway is a dark gravel line across wet silver. Marl Sedge rises out of the reeds twenty paces off, so quietly that two guards reach for their swords.

Her report is short and flat, like everything she says.

"About midnight a longboat landed five at the creek mouth, past the boat-shed. A man in a brown coat, and four hands with pikes and hand crossbows. At dawn a second boat brought a tall man in a grey cloak, hooded. He stood on the shed roof two hours looking at the road, and then went inside." She wipes her hands on her cloak. "They've dragged a coil of heavy chain and two boat-anchors out of the shed and hidden them in the grass at the far end of the causeway. I can't swear to it, but it looks like a drag. They block the culvert and trap whatever is on the road." She pauses. "Your reeds on the stake path were scattered. Someone's used it. I didn't see the Heron's Tithe herself. She may be up the creek behind the shed."

So Corvin's tip was true, or true enough. It is twelve forty. The causeway opens properly about two, and your wagon is due to start across around half past, to reach the culvert as the water drops. You have three slots, three Inspirations, Kit, Pell, six guards, one tracker, a bait tube in your saddlebag, and a drag-chain waiting at the far end. The grey cloak is waiting for you. What does Wren do?

sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. About 3 AM a taller figure, hooded, was rowed ashore alone for an hour and spoke with Sparrow; Marl could not hear or see his face. Before dawn he left again by the same skiff. At first light a grey sail showed far out beyond the creek mouth. Marl also found on the landward side a cold fire-pit and fresh trampled reed, where she hadn't expected anyone: the enemy has scouted the landward bank too. You mount Ember, check the tube one last time, and ride up beside the wagon. "One word to anyone on the road that isn't in the plan," you murmur to Corvin, "and Pell gags you." You give the order and the little column moves out, with Kit beside you and the wagon's wheels grinding on the dike road. You hum the road song as you go, low, so that the guards behind you hear it and ease a little in their saddles. It is a quiet, grey ride with no sign of anyone following. Seven hours of steady road take you across fields and through two small villages, and a little after noon the flats open up ahead and the causeway lies before you. It is a long dark line across the mud, still half under the slack water.

Marl Sedge is waiting at the landward end, so quiet that you almost ride past her. She comes out of the reeds with mud to her knees and gives her report in a flat, careful whisper.

"Dusk yesterday, a skiff landed at the far boat-shed. Five of them: the lean man in brown, Sparrow, and four hands with pikes. They stayed the night and ate cold. About three in the morning a taller man, hooded, was rowed ashore alone for an hour and spoke with the brown one. I couldn't hear or see his face. He went back out before dawn." She wipes her mouth. "At first light there was a grey sail far out past the creek mouth. And this side." She nods at the reeds. "There's a cold fire-pit and fresh trampled reed in the place I'd have picked for your guards. Somebody scouted the landward bank, too. I don't think they saw me."

It's eighteen minutes past noon. The causeway opens about two. You have six guards, Pell, Kit, Marl, Corvin in the wagon, and the tube. The enemy has at least five at the far end, and has probably marked the landward reeds as well. What does Wren do?

input.add_to_description: Day 15 ~12:30 PM, Marl Sedge's report from the far-bank boat-shed (she watched all night, unseen): a grey-sailed longboat landed at dusk Day 14 with Sparrow (brown coat), six armed hands (four pikes, two crossbows), and, after midnight, the tall hooded Grey Cloak, who walked the causeway's far end alone by lantern and spoke to Sparrow about 'the middle, at the turn'. They sleep in the drowned boat-shed. A skiff with two men crosses the channel upstream at dawn to the landward bank to scout the reeds: Marl watched them come within a stone's throw of where the guards would lie, then withdraw; they know the reeds are a danger. Wren's reed tell at the stake: broken, used. The enemy plans to take the wagon at the culvert when it stops at the middle.

entries.text: notebook: updated Gannet Causeway

You ride up beside the wagon and murmur your warning. Corvin gives you a mild look from the bench. "Child, I have never spoken out of turn in my life. I have only spoken in other people's." Pell, on his big grey, doesn't look round, but you notice he has moved his horse a length closer to the wagon.

The column moves out in good order, with Kit on your left, the wagon in the middle, and the six guards in their grey cloaks trailing. You hum the road song low, and after a mile the guards are humming along with you. It is a long, bright morning on the Marrowford road. The land flattens into marsh and reed, and the smell of salt grows stronger. A little after half past twelve you reach the landward end of the Gannet Causeway. The water is falling, the gravel is showing, and the road runs out into the flats like a pale thread, nine hundred paces to the far bank. In the middle a stone culvert squeezes it narrow.

Marl is waiting in the reeds, so still that Kit's horse doesn't notice her until she speaks. She is grey with mud and tiredness, and her report is short and flat.

"Last night, after you went, a grey-sailed longboat came in to the boat-shed. Sparrow, the brown coat. Six hands, four pikes and two crossbows. After midnight a tall hooded man walked the far end of the causeway alone with a lantern. I heard him say to Sparrow, 'the middle, at the turn.' They slept in the shed." She wipes her mouth. "At dawn two men crossed upstream in a skiff and came to within a stone's throw of where the guards would lie, in the reeds. They saw the cover. They went back." She meets your eye. "Your reed tell at the stake was broken. They used it."

So the enemy knows about the reeds, and they plan to take the wagon in the middle, at the culvert, when the water is lowest. They number eight at least: Sparrow, six hands, and the Grey Cloak. You have Kit, Pell, six guards, Corvin in the wagon, and the afternoon ebb.

It is half past twelve. The causeway will be clear around two, and the enemy is waiting for it. You have three slots, three Inspirations, 17 hit points, and a plan that has been half read. What does Wren do?

entries.text: notebook: updated The Bait Wagon

"One word that isn't in the plan, and Pell gags you," you murmur as you pull Ember alongside the wagon. Corvin inclines his head, gravely amused. "I shall be a model of discretion." The column moves out in the early morning light, with Pell at the wagon's head, six grey-cloaked guards behind, Kit at your shoulder, and you humming the road song low enough that it steadies the guards without carrying. The back road is dull and quiet, and nobody follows you. You reach the landward end of the causeway at half past eleven.

The flats are brimming still. The high tide of a little before eleven has left the causeway just awash, and the water is shining pale and slack over it. Marl Sedge rises from the reeds like a heron standing up, plastered with salt mud. She was never seen, and her report is clear and unsparing.

At dusk last night a skiff landed three men at the far-bank boat-shed. At about midnight the Heron's Tithe's longboat brought three more, and one of them was tall and hooded in a grey cloak. That makes six: Sparrow, four hands (one with a longbow), and the Grey Cloak himself, who has stayed inside the boat-shed. At first light two hands waded out to the culvert in the middle of the causeway and fixed something under it, a coil of rope and a pulley-frame. She thinks it's a net or a rope-trap that can be sprung across the road's narrow place to snare a wagon. The reeds you scattered on the path to the mooring-stake were scattered further: the stake was used. They haven't seen the Vantry guards. They haven't seen Marl.

So the trap is real, and Corvin's advice was right, or was meant to look right. It is half past eleven. The causeway opens in about two and a half hours, and the enemy knows the tide as well as you do. You've three slots, three Inspirations, six guards, Pell, Kit, Marl, and a tube holding a lure. What does Wren do?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

line:
"Kit, get to the barn door and help the guards pull the prisoners out, and keep Corvin and Ansel together where you can see both. The fire is a lure, and the real move is behind the north hedge."

I run along the barn's shadow toward the north side, plant myself with my back to the wall so nothing can come up behind me, and cast Faerie Fire on the dark stretch of hedge where the burning rag came from, lighting up any hidden shapes. At the same time I shout, "Sparrow! You smile too much to be a good thief, so show yourself!"

What does Wren do?

sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

input.add_to_description: Day 17 night: Wren sent a rider ahead to Lord Edric with a warning note ("Sparrow comes to Osric, bar the chapel and keep him inside the manor. W."). At first light on Day 18 Wren, Kit and two fast guards ride ahead for Thornhallow; Pell follows with the wagon and prisoners.

entries.text: notebook: updated Sparrow
sheet: money -1 sp 5 cp: now 71 gp 1 sp 9 cp

You climb down off the table, press a coin into the drover's hand, and draw Kit and Pell into the corner by the stairs. Pell listens with his jaw working, then nods. "Two of my best, Tarn and Edda, on the fast horses. I'll bring the wagon and the prisoners behind. Slower, but I'll not lose them." He doesn't like splitting the column, and he says so once. He doesn't argue after that.

You pay a few coppers for a bed in the loft and a bit more for the innkeeper's ink and a scrap of paper. Then you write: "Sparrow comes to Osric, bar the chapel and keep him inside the manor. W." You seal it with a dab of your own wax. A stable boy on the inn's swiftest pony takes it into the dark with a silver penny in his fist. He swears he'll be at Thornhallow's gate by the small hours. You check Ember's feed and shoes and count your slots (three) and your Inspirations (three). Then you sleep.

You wake at six on Day 18 to a grey, cold dawn. Your hit points are full at 17, and Kit is saddled and waiting with Tarn and Edda, two lean guards in Vantry grey on rangy horses. Pell has the wagon loaded, and Corvin, Ansel and Tam Rudd are in it. Ansel meets your eyes once and then looks at the road.

You're away at the gallop, and Thornhallow should be in sight by midday if nothing slows you. You have 71 gp, 1 sp and 9 cp. What does Wren do?

input.add_to_description: Day 18 dusk, Thornhallow study (Edric, Osric, Wren, Kit present): Ansel told Edric to his face that he is the son of Hugh Verrel and Joan, a chapel servant, wed in secret. Hugh did not drown: Aldous Verrel sent him away and had him struck from the paper when he refused a match; Hugh died abroad of fever when Ansel was a child. Ansel was raised by Joan's kin and told his name was a shame. He claims no manor; he says he wanted the founding lamp and his father's name written back. Edric, shaken, did not answer. Corvin was held in the gatehouse under guard.

entries.text: notebook: updated Ansel Verrel
time: 50 minutes later: Day 18, 6:35:06 PM

You go down to the yard and find Pell grey with dust. At your word he sends Corvin to the gatehouse under two spears and gives Ansel two guards for the stair. You walk Ansel to the study door yourself. His chains clink on every step, and he says nothing the whole way.

"He's ready to tell it his own way, my lord," you say. "Ansel, say it plain. Let Osric hear every word."

You ask Lyle to hold the chest unopened until the clerk comes, and to open it at noon before herself and a notary. Then you borrow two fast horses from the bridge-house stable, with a lean watchman named Perrin on a third. "Back by dusk," you tell her.

Your Survival is a 20. A hand-cart rut is easy to find once you know its weight. This one cuts deep into the road mud, so the cart was heavily loaded. It is fresh, since the edges haven't crumbled, and it is pulled by a man, with a boot-scuff on every stride. Two sets of boots walk beside it, one narrow and one broad. Near a milestone a hard, neat stride joins them, a man who walks a little pigeon-toed. Three miles out, the ruts turn off down a farm lane toward the river.

At the lane's end is Coldwharf, an old timber wharf with a long boat-store of weathered boards. The cart stands unhitched by the door, still with its tarpaulin tied down. The door is shut. A thin thread of smoke rises from a roof-hole, not a cooking fire's smoke but the dry, curling grey of burning paper. Nothing else moves. The river slides past the pilings.

You get down and walk both for an hour. Pip finds a broken cart-pin in the lane, which could mean anything. Nothing says which way the cart went.

input.add_to_description: Day 20: Wren, Kit and a watchman followed the hand-cart rut out of Marrowford's east gate (Survival 21): the cart was heavy, left before dusk on Day 19, and turned off the east road onto the old tow-path toward the river reaches two miles out, then the trail was lost in the reed-lined shallows where a flat-bottomed boat was pulled up (stern-drag marks, a dropped sealing-wax lump). You ask Lyle to hold the chest unopened until the clerk comes. "If he arrives at noon, he opens it in front of you and a notary, and I'll be back by dusk." She nods and lends you two fast horses and a young watchman named Pip. You, Kit and Pip ride out the east gate.

The rut is easy to read, and your Survival is a 21. The cart was heavy, with deep wheels and a lopsided load, and it passed before dusk yesterday. Two miles out it leaves the east road and bumps onto the old tow-path toward the river reaches. You follow it through the willows and onto a reedy shore, and there it ends. The ground is churned, a flat-bottomed boat has been dragged up and pushed off again (the stern left a long groove), and a lump of green sealing wax lies in the mud, dropped in a hurry. The river takes the trail from there, downstream or upstream, and you can't tell which.

The gate-keeper at the east road is another matter. Your Persuasion is a natural 1. You ask too eagerly, too cleverly, and he decides you are a busybody. He shuts his mouth, and you see him send a boy off to the gate captain with word that a stranger is asking after a man with a notched ear. If Crake has friends in Marrowford, they'll hear of it by evening.

Kit crouches by the groove and says in her dry way, "Cart's gone, and so's the boat. They had a day's start and a river." Pip looks over the water uneasily.

It's twenty past twelve on Day 20. You have 17 of 17 hit points, three slots and three Inspirations, and 78 gp. Dame Crowe's clerk should now be opening the chest at the bridge-house. What does Wren do?
